title: Destemming and whole bunch
what: For red Lots: whether the grapes go into the vat fully destemmed, or with 30 % or 100 % of the bunches left whole, stems and all.

steps: A larger share of whole bunches
brings more stems into the vat
so tannin and stalky notes rise with the share; in a Pinot Noir trial the clear rises came at 60 % and above

choose: 100 % whole bunch gives a spicier, more structured Pinot Noir: the stems add tannin, and the uncrushed berries ferment partly inside the skin, which brightens the red fruit. Unripe stems taste bitter and green. 30 % gives a subtler version; fully destemmed keeps the most colour.
exam: Questions ask how and why whole-bunch fermentation changes a red, usually Pinot Noir. Name each effect (stem tannin, fermentation inside the berry, aroma, colour), say why the stems must be ripe, and tie it to the style.

check.question: Cool year: Pinot Noir seeds 50 % ripe, stems green. What does 100 % whole bunch add, compared with destemmed?
options: Firmer, coarser tannin and stalky, green notes
Nothing measurable: only seeds give tannin
check.answer: Firmer, coarser tannin and stalky, green notes
check.why: Stems give up tannin and green-smelling compounds, most of all when unripe; in trials they also lowered the colour.

simplification: Game simplification: the game does not lower colour for whole bunches or model the fresher fruit from fermentation inside the berry; stem tannin rises with the whole-bunch share, and stalky notes come from unripe stems, judged by the seeds' ripeness.
